title: A Dying Sun-Like Star, Carved Into a Lion
hook: Webb's infrared view of NGC 2392 shows what our own Sun will do at the end: a naked white-hot core blasting radiation into the gas it just shed.
key_points: NGC 2392, the Lion Nebula, is a planetary nebula — the shell of gas a dying Sun-like star throws off, not anything to do with planets.
James Webb imaged it in the infrared, which sees through dust that blocks visible light.
At the centre sits a white dwarf: the exposed, scorching core left when the star's outer layers departed.
Radiation from that core is excavating the surrounding gas and dust, sculpting the lion-like face.
The 'mane' is a sprawl of dusty clumps dense enough to have resisted being blown away.
content_html: Stars like the Sun do not explode. They swell, grow unstable, and shrug off their outer layers, leaving the naked core behind — and it is the glow of that shed gas, lit from within, that we call a planetary nebula. The name is a leftover from early telescopes, in which the round shapes looked planet-like; there are no planets involved.
extra_html: NGC 2392, the Lion Nebula, is one such object, and James Webb has now imaged it in the infrared, a band that sees past the dust which obscures visible light. Reported via ScienceDaily, the view shows a white dwarf at the centre — the exposed, still-scorching core of a star not unlike our own — pumping radiation outward into the gas it recently expelled. That radiation does the sculpting: it excavates and ionises the surrounding material, carving the lion's face, while a sprawling "mane" of dustier, denser clumps has held out against being swept away. It is a portrait of a specific object and also a preview, since the Sun is destined to end the same way.

related.title: The Life Cycle of Stars
related.hook: Stars are born in collapsing gas clouds, spend their lives fusing hydrogen into helium, then die in ways that depend entirely on how heavy they are.

related.title: Dying Stars Can Kick Themselves Across Space
related.hook: A dying star flinging off lopsided blobs of gas nudges itself with each one — thousands of tiny kicks that add up to a getaway of about a kilometer per second.

related.title: Four White Dwarfs Were Hiding in Plain Sight Nearby
related.hook: Four white dwarf stars sat undetected for decades, drowned out by the glare of their brighter red dwarf companions — until Hubble's ultraviolet eyes finally caught them.

flashcards.explanation_html: The name is a historical accident from how they looked in early telescopes. NGC 2392 is gas thrown off by a dying Sun-like star, with a white dwarf at its centre.

flashcards.prompt: What is left at the centre of NGC 2392, and what is it doing to the nebula?
flashcards.back_html: A scorching white dwarf — the star's exposed core — whose radiation is carving out the surrounding gas and dust into the nebula's lion-like shape.

flashcards.prompt: Why observe a nebula like this in the infrared?
flashcards.back_html: Infrared light penetrates the dust that blocks visible light, revealing structure such as the nebula's surviving dusty clumps.
